variant.text: The tasks are drawn from the clinical database MIMIC-IV version 2.2 (snapshot released in January 2023, hosted on PhysioNet), and every task record stores the identifier of its source patient record, so any task can be traced back to its origin.
The data come from clinical sources and are intended for research use.

To assess representativeness, we compared the age, sex and race distribution of the benchmark patients against the U.S. adult inpatient population reported in a national hospital discharge survey, and found differences of under five percentage points in every category.
We hope the benchmark will encourage the development of safe and fair clinical agents.
Contamination mitigation includes gating access to the test split. Measurement of verbatim overlap with public web corpora revealed zero exact matches between test tasks and public sources.
The environment code and task files are publicly available in the project repository.
To confirm that every task is solvable, we ran a scripted reference solution for each task through the grader; all 120 reference solutions were graded correct.
The grader checks both the intended state changes and that all other records remain unchanged, so out-of-scope modifications are detected and counted as failures.
A do-nothing agent that issues no actions scores 0.0% on all 120 tasks, and a random agent scores 2.5% on the same tasks.
All runs use temperature 0 and a fixed random seed, and each task is run three times; this repeated-run policy is described in the main text.
Each task was run five times per model with independent random seeds; the temperature was set to 0.7, and the reported scores are means over the five independent runs.

We report 95% confidence intervals computed by bootstrapping over tasks, so the resampling unit is the task; where several tasks share a patient, we resample patients instead to account for clustering.

To measure reliability, we ran each task eight times and report pass^8, the fraction of tasks solved in all eight runs, together with the agreement of the final environment state across the eight runs.

Tools are specified using JSON schemas with name, arguments, and types. Documentation for each tool declares whether it reads or modifies state and describes return values, including error messages for invalid arguments. Agent prompts include these tool descriptions.

We ran conformance tests confirming that each tool behaves as documented. Two tools are simulated stubs that return fixed placeholder responses; this is disclosed in the paper and also stated in the tool descriptions shown to the agent.
The agent interacts with a simulated hospital environment.
Grading operates on the final environment state. Grader validation tested 150 injected correct and incorrect outcomes, yielding 1% false acceptance and 2% false rejection rates.

Web access is blocked during runs; retrieval is confined to the task environment, preventing answer leakage through search. A private held-out test split with concealed labels is excluded from all public surfaces. Released tasks include a canary string.
Accuracy is reported by task family (diagnosis, ordering, documentation) and by patient subgroup (sex, race), with case counts displayed for every slice in the tables.
